name: CA3140AMZ96
title: CA3140, CA3140A: 4.5 MHz BiMOS operational amplifier with MOSFET input and bipolar output
summary: A single op amp that pairs a gate-protected PMOS input pair with a bipolar output on one die, for very high input impedance (1.5 TΩ) and input currents near 10 pA. It runs from 4 V to 36 V, single or split, its inputs reach 0.5 V below the negative rail, and its output swings close to V-, so it suits single-supply work and replaces the 741 in most sockets. It is internally compensated for unity gain, with terminals for offset nulling, extra compensation and an output strobe. CA3140A is the tighter offset grade; CA3140AMZ96 is the CA3140A in SOIC-8 on a 2,500-piece reel.

circuits.title: Figure 1. Zener clamp on terminals 8 and 4 limiting the output swing to TTL levels
circuits.description: A 6.2 V zener from the strobe terminal (8) to V- (4) caps how far the output can rise, so the CA3140 can drive a TTL gate input directly while its own supply is anywhere from 5 V to 36 V. The highest output is the zener voltage less two base-emitter drops inside the chip, whatever the supply.

parts.note: any TTL input; second input held near 5 V

circuits.title: Figure 3A. Offset voltage nulling, basic
circuits.description: A 10 kΩ potentiometer spans the two offset-null terminals (1 and 5) with its wiper returned to V- (4). This covers far more adjustment than the offset needs, so much of the rotation goes unused.

circuits.title: Figure 3B. Offset voltage nulling, improved resolution
circuits.description: Same as the basic method, with a fixed resistor R between each null terminal and its end of the 10 kΩ potentiometer. The resistors narrow the range so the whole rotation is useful; typical values are 4.7 kΩ (CA3140) and 18 kΩ (CA3140A).

circuits.title: Figure 3C. Offset voltage nulling, simpler improved resolution
circuits.description: The 10 kΩ potentiometer spans terminals 1 and 5 and a single resistor R, of about 4.7 kΩ (CA3140) or 18 kΩ (CA3140A), joins its wiper to V-. For a potentiometer whose track does not reach 0 Ω at the ends, R is taken 10 % below that value.

circuits.title: Figure 4. Driving a triac from the output sinking capability (120 VAC)
circuits.description: The CA3140 runs from a supply taken off the 120 VAC line through RS and a series diode, held on a capacitor (about 30 V with no load). Its output drives the triac gate through RL and a series diode; a shunt diode from the gate node to the low line keeps negative surges at the gate away from the amplifier. Because the output stage pulls nearly to V-, no level shifter is needed.

parts.note: polarised; supply about 30 V at no load

circuits.title: Figure 4. Driving an NPN power transistor from the output
circuits.description: The output drives the base of an NPN transistor through RL; the transistor switches a load from a separate high-voltage rail. The emitter and the CA3140 V- terminal share ground, so the output swing down to V- turns the transistor fully off.

circuits.title: Figure 5B. Settling time test circuit, voltage follower
circuits.description: Unity-gain follower on ±15 V. The source feeds the non-inverting input through 10 kΩ; 2 kΩ in parallel with 0.05 µF returns the output to the inverting input. Each supply pin has 0.1 µF to ground and the output carries a 100 pF and 2 kΩ simulated load.

circuits.title: Figure 5B. Settling time test circuit, inverting unity gain
circuits.description: Inverting amplifier of gain -1 (5 kΩ in, 5 kΩ feedback) on ±15 V with the non-inverting input grounded. A divider from the input node through a 200 Ω trimmer and 4.99 kΩ, and from the output through 5.11 kΩ, meets at the settling point, which two 1N914 diodes clamp to ground in both directions. The output carries 100 pF and 2 kΩ.

parts.note: trimmer with its wiper tied to one end

circuits.title: Figure 10A. Function generator
circuits.description: A CA3080A transconductance amplifier charges a timing capacitor; the CA3140 buffers the resulting triangle as a non-inverting readout; a CA3080 wired as a fast hysteresis switch squares it and feeds the square wave straight back to the CA3080A input, closing the loop. The current into the CA3080A bias terminal (5) sets the frequency over a 1,000,000 to 1 range, from a potentiometer network or from the optional buffer of Figure 11. Four 1N914 diodes at the switch output fix its level and, with the divider at the CA3080 inverting input, the triangle amplitude. A 7 pF to 60 pF trimmer sets high-frequency ramp linearity and another the high-frequency level.

circuits.title: Figure 11. Meter driver and buffer amplifier
circuits.description: The CA3140, powered between ground and -15 V, is a low-impedance follower that sets the voltage on the CA3080A bias terminal of the Figure 10 generator, so the frequency control works smoothly. Its feedback is taken after a 4.7 kΩ output resistor. A 200 µA meter, fed through 620 Ω and a 1 kΩ sensitivity trimmer and returned through three transistors of a CA3086 array, reads that voltage; since the CA3080A output current changes about one decade per 60 mV of bias voltage, the meter gives a logarithmic frequency scale (six decades in 360 mV). The array transistors also supply a reference that sets the meter low end and tracks the temperature drift of the CA3080A bias terminal.

circuits.title: Figure 12. Sine wave shaper
circuits.description: The CA3140 is a voltage follower whose feedback network uses diodes of a CA3019 array to bend the triangle from the function generator into a sine wave with typically under 2 % THD. The zero-crossing slope comes from the 10 kΩ control R3 between terminals 2 and 6 and from 9.1 kΩ plus R1 from terminal 2 to ground. Diodes D1 to D4 add two break points; D5 and D6 give positive feedback that flattens the peaks, needed because a follower cannot fall to zero gain by itself.

circuits.title: Figure 14. Wideband output amplifier
circuits.description: A high slew rate line driver for 50 Ω. The CA3140 drives a complementary emitter-follower pair (2N3053, 2N4037) biased by two 1N914 diodes, with 2.7 Ω emitter resistors and a 51 Ω, 2 W series output resistor. Feedback is 1.8 kΩ shunted by 2 pF to the inverting input, which has 200 Ω to ground and a DC level adjustment through 3 kΩ; 2.4 pF between terminals 1 and 8 adds compensation. Nominal bandwidth 10 MHz, rise time 35 ns. With the function generator and sine shaper it gives 18 Vp-p open circuit or 9 Vp-p into 50 Ω, which needs 28 V/µs.

circuits.description: From one input supply, a resistor feeds a reference; a potentiometer across it sets the CA3140 non-inverting input. circuits.title: Figure 16. Regulated power supply

The offset is multiplied by the gain, so a 100 kΩ null control is fitted.

circuits.title: Figure 19. Tone control circuit (20 dB midband gain), single supply
circuits.description: Non-inverting tone control: the signal enters the non-inverting input through 0.005 µF, and the tone network sits between the output and ground with its centre on the inverting input. Wideband gain is the maximum boost or cut plus one, in this case eleven (20 dB flat); bass and treble boost and cut are ±15 dB at 100 Hz and 10 kHz; 25 Vp-p output at 20 kHz; -3 dB at 24 kHz from 1 kHz. With 20 dB boost and cut, the input loading is essentially the resistance from terminal 3 to ground. Single 30 V supply: two 2.2 MΩ resistors bias a mid-supply point (decoupled by 0.1 µF) that feeds the non-inverting input through 5.1 MΩ.

circuits.title: Figure 21. Basic Wien bridge oscillator using an operational amplifier
circuits.description: A series R2-C2 from the output and a parallel R1-C1 to ground form the frequency-setting arm at the non-inverting input; RF and RS set the closed-loop gain. With R1 = R2 and C1 = C2 the loop needs a gain of 3. RS is usually a variable element (FET channel, thermistor, lamp) whose resistance moves with output amplitude to hold the level.

circuits.title: Figure 22. Wien bridge oscillator circuit using CA3140
circuits.description: Wien bridge oscillator with 1000 pF capacitors and R1 = R2 = R chosen for the frequency. Amplitude is held by a monolithic zener and diode bridge (a diode array) in the feedback path: as the output grows the zener conducts more, adding feedback and lowering gain. The combination tends toward a zero temperature coefficient and, having no time constant, sets no lower frequency limit (1 µF polycarbonate capacitors with 22 MΩ give 0.007 Hz). Output 19 Vp-p to 22 Vp-p, THD under 0.3 %. Amplitude must fall as frequency rises to stay within the slew rate: 180 kHz at 16 Vp-p needs about 9 V/µs.

parts.note: diode bridge on 8, 6, 2, 5; diode 9 to 1; zener 3 to 4; terminal 7 is the substrate

notes: R for each frequency: 50 Hz, 3.3 MΩ; 100 Hz, 1.6 MΩ; 1 kHz, 160 MΩ; 10 kHz, 16 MΩ; 30 kHz, 5.1 MΩ. The last three read MΩ where f = 1/(2πRC) with 1000 pF gives kΩ (160 kΩ, 16 kΩ, 5.3 kΩ).

circuits.title: Figure 23. Sample and hold circuit
circuits.description: A CA3080A acts as input buffer and low-feedthrough switch, driven by a strobe (0 V samples, -15 V holds) through 30 kΩ; it charges the 200 pF storage capacitor C1 (with 400 Ω in series), and the CA3140 reads the capacitor out and nulls the system offset with its 100 kΩ control. Slew rate is 0.5 mA / 200 pF = 2.5 V/µs; droop in hold is 170 pA / 200 pF = 0.85 V/s, 170 pA being the CA3080A leakage when strobed off. A 2000 pF capacitor would give 0.085 V/s droop and 0.25 V/µs slew. The anti-parallel 1N914 pair between CA3080A terminal 3 and the CA3140 output keeps large input signals from feeding through to C1 during hold.

operation.text: Two class A stages give the voltage gain and a class AB stage the output current. A bias circuit holds cascoded constant currents in the first two stages; an on-chip 12 pF capacitor compensates the amplifier for unity-gain follower use.

PMOS transistors Q9 and Q10 form the differential pair, loaded by the bipolar mirror Q11, Q12 with R2 to R5, which also converts to single-ended drive for the second stage. Q2 and Q5 in cascode are its current source. Small diodes D3 to D5 guard the gate oxide against high-voltage transients such as static discharge.

Q13 with its cascode load Q3, Q4 provides most of the gain; C1 sets the on-chip compensation. A small capacitor between terminals 1 and 8 adds Miller roll-off where wanted. It lowers the open-loop bandwidth and the slew rate in proportion: 20 % less bandwidth costs about 20 % of slew rate.

Pulling terminal 8 to terminal 4, mechanically or electrically, forces the output to about the terminal 4 potential. The sink current needed is 220 µA typical at ±15 V and 200 µA at 5 V. The high impedance of terminal 8 lets a small-signal transistor do current limiting in a regulator.

Emitter followers Q17, Q18 source current from V+ through D7, R9 and R11, their quiescent current mirrored from D2 via Q14, Q15. Sinking is done by Q16, a dynamic current sink driven by output-level sensing through PMOS Q21: when the output must fall, Q16 sinks in proportion to the change, whatever the load. Q19 limits short-circuit current by diverting drive when the drop across R11 grows.

All quiescent currents except the dynamic sink follow the current in R1. D1, mirrored with Q1 to Q3, senses the Q6 emitter current and trims the Q6 base drive to hold a constant current through Q6, Q8 and D2. D1 also fixes the Q2 and Q3 currents, and D2 fixes those of Q14 and Q15.

Input common-mode range and output swing complement each other, so the amplifier works from a single supply down to 4 V and keeps the correct output phase when an input goes below terminal 4, which matters in comparators. With 2 V dual supplies the lower end of the input range is below ground.

A current regulator referenced to the PMOS threshold keeps the operating current, and so performance, fairly steady at low supply. The limit comes just below 4 V total, where the top of the input common-mode range reaches terminal 4. The output range also extends toward the negative rail but stays slightly above the input range.

A 6.2 V zener from terminal 8 to terminal 4 confines the output to TTL levels. Because the output sinks to V-, it can drive power transistors and thyristors without level shifting; a series resistor RL limits the drive, and a series plus shunt diode at a thyristor gate keeps negative surges off the amplifier.

A 10 kΩ potentiometer across terminals 1 and 5 with the wiper to terminal 4 nulls the offset with range to spare. Series resistors at each end (typically 4.7 kΩ for CA3140, 18 kΩ for CA3140A) use the rotation better; alternatively one such resistor from the wiper to V- does the same, taken 10 % lower for a potentiometer that does not reach 0 Ω.

Inputs may go below terminal 4, but a series resistor should keep input current under 1 mA to protect the input network. In a unity-gain follower some resistance belongs between the output and the inverting input so that a large input transient cannot push through the protection into the internal current source and cause positive feedback; 3.9 kΩ suffices.
Input current is about 10 pA with the inputs centred at nominal dissipation. Load current raises dissipation and chip temperature, and the input current rises with it.

Large differential input voltages held for long periods at high temperature shift the MOSFET offset slightly. Voltage and temperature speed the change; it reverses with opposite stress. At 85 °C the shift is much smaller than at 125 °C, and with small symmetrical differential signals it is comparable to that of a bipolar-input amplifier.
Settling is fast because the amplifier has both high open-loop gain and a wide bandwidth.

Constant loop gain at every setting keeps regulation constant. Series pass transistors with high ICBO, and the VCE(sat) of the CA3140 output, can stop the output reaching zero. The D2201 sense diode gives more sensitivity from its higher forward drop but needs heat sinking, since 1 A at 1 V is a watt that shifts the trip point; mounting the sensing transistor near it helps with the diode temperature coefficient. Where temperature stability of the limit matters, a sense resistor is preferred. Turn-on is slow because the reference rises slowly.
